overview: Botswana’s history includes many communities and languages. Colonial Bechuanaland became an independent republic in 1966. Family teaching, craft businesses, schools and community museums reveal histories that continue beyond changes of government.

periods.title: Within the Bechuanaland Protectorate
periods.summary: Britain proclaimed the protectorate in 1885 and extended it northward in 1890. The map’s 1920 opening belongs within that colonial period; it is not the founding date of an independent Botswana.

periods.title: Preparing for independence
periods.summary: The Attorney General’s office, previously based in Mafikeng in South Africa, had moved to Gaberones by 1965. The relocation brought this part of colonial administration into the territory that would soon become independent.

periods.title: An independent republic
periods.summary: On 30 September 1966, Bechuanaland became the Republic of Botswana. Seretse Khama, previously prime minister, became its first president. Independence changed the government’s constitutional position, while communities continued their everyday lives.

periods.title: Building educational opportunities
periods.summary: A national appeal in 1976 raised support for expanding the university campus in Botswana. The effort connected higher education with public contributions and aspirations for the country’s future.

periods.title: Living traditions and protected heritage
periods.summary: Tsodilo entered the World Heritage List in 2001. Its archaeology, paintings and continuing sacred associations bring different kinds of history together. Recognizing the site does not assign one date or meaning to every painting.

items.text: Among the Bakgatla ba Kgafela in Kgatleng, UNESCO’s 2012 account describes women shaping pots by hand. They build from the base toward the rim, smooth the clay with a wooden paddle and fire the finished vessels in a pit kiln. A useful pot begins well before dinner: preparing the earth, shaping it and firing it all take skill.

The same account describes daughters and granddaughters learning by watching experienced potters and practising. Pots serve several household purposes, including storing water, cooking and fermenting sorghum beer. This is education through repeated, practical work. UNESCO also recorded difficulties passing on the craft as experienced makers became fewer and cheaper mass-produced containers competed with their pots.

Basket maker Thitaku Kushanya recalls starting at home in Etsha 6 when she was five, learning from her mother. She says she sold her first basket at eight for one pula and fifty thebe. This is her own remembered childhood, not a rule about when all children learned. A carefully made basket could be both a family lesson and a first sale.

Research published in 2017 describes women weaving together in courtyards while children played nearby. In interviews, makers explained how sales paid for food, schooling and healthcare. The basket on a shop shelf was therefore connected to conversation, patient work and household budgets. These accounts come from particular communities in Ngamiland, rather than a survey of every family in Botswana.

The study photographs patterns called Ribs of the Giraffe and Flight of the Swallow in baskets from Gumare and Maun. Makers used narrow palm strips, coloured with roots and bark. One photograph shows a needle opening a hole for the next stitch. The animal belongs to the design: no giraffe is required in the sewing kit.

The Kavora women’s basketry collective explains that its name comes from its home ward within the Etsha villages. Putting that name on a basket identifies the people and place behind it. The group connects sharing its craft with its ambition to provide a sustainable livelihood for daughters and granddaughters. A basket can carry a maker’s hopes for the future as well as a pattern.

sections.title: Learning, with a little help from cattle

items.text: Botswana’s 1976 university appeal invited public support for a larger campus. The university later recorded donations of cattle, money, grain and eggs. Contributions took forms that different households could offer. The campaign is remembered in a statue outside the library. A university can begin with books and building plans, but in this case its fundraising history also includes a herd.

At Swaneng Hill near Serowe, Patrick van Rensburg developed an approach linking secondary education with practical skills. An account written in 1999 explains that its associated brigades offered school-leavers work and training in construction trades. Lessons could involve making and building as well as reading. This was a particular educational experiment, not the curriculum of every Botswana school.

sections.title: A new country, and a very big evening

items.text: For part of the colonial period, the Attorney General’s office serving Bechuanaland was in Mafikeng, across the border in South Africa. Its own institutional history records a move to Gaberones by 1965. Following an office’s address can reveal political change: administrative work was moving into the territory as independence approached. The older spelling Gaberones refers to today’s Gaborone.

A contemporary Kutlwano announcement looked ahead to independence celebrations in September 1966. It promised hilltop bonfires as the new flag replaced the British flag at midnight leading into 30 September. Reading the announcement brings the anticipation into view: the political change was also being planned as a public occasion. It records what organizers intended, rather than proving every planned bonfire took place.

A women’s club in the BORAVAST area, active from the late 1960s, brought together activities such as sewing, crochet and baking bread. Research completed in 2024 traces how this work developed into a community museum project, with fundraising and local partnerships. A museum’s story can begin with people making useful things together, rather than with a royal collection.

The Tsodilo hills preserve thousands of rock paintings alongside a much longer archaeological record. UNESCO describes traces of human activity across at least 100,000 years, with gaps. That does not make all the paintings 100,000 years old. Their individual dates are often uncertain, and the painted record extends into much more recent centuries. Different kinds of evidence keep different clocks.

Tsodilo is also a sacred landscape for Hambukushu and San communities. UNESCO records continuing associations with ancestral spirits, hills and water holes. Archaeologists study physical traces, while communities maintain relationships with the place. These are distinct kinds of knowledge, and a heritage designation does not turn a living sacred place into merely an outdoor picture gallery.

ending.text: British rule ended with independence on 30 September 1966. Botswana continues as a republic. The older map record’s endpoint in 1938 and the later record’s opening in 1960 are coverage dates, not the disappearance and rebirth of the country’s people.
